Zach is a polite person, but his grading is extremely harsh, and the way he conducts the course is, frankly, poorly structured. As translation students, why are we expected to study American culture through literary-style texts as if we were literature majors? Why are we forced to read and analyze a new text every single week?

Zach often assumes we already know everything and skips over crucial parts, which creates frustrating gaps between topics and makes it harder for students to truly understand what’s being taught. I’m sure he knows a lot, but he seriously struggles when it comes to conveying that knowledge clearly and effectively. American culture could not have been taught in a more confusing and dull way.

Moreover, this is a 3-credit course, and according to university policy, students are allowed 30% absence—which equals around 10 hours. Yet Zach unfairly limited us to just 7 hours and even threatened to prevent us from taking the final exam. 7 hours equals 90% attendance, and denying students their right to take the exam based on this is simply unjust.

This course does give guidelines for us to-be-translators so I acknowledge that it is necessary however, if the instructor was uninterested in making the courses interactive, the course would be unbearably boring. And my biggest critique of this course is that it focuses on the Western, European side a lot more than other parts of the world. There were mentions of Chinese and Arabic translations here and there but I found them insufficient. I understand that since our department is on two western languages, English and French, but I still think we should learn more about the other parts more, as who knows, their ideas might fit our style no matter how different the languages are. I found the Reading Responses to be very useful, as it did kindly force students to read at least one reading of the week. And the response part itself required us to truly think about these theories, as our instructor didn't want us to summarize, but to write about our questions, impressions, things we agree and we disagree. It felt more free and made the readings have a longer-impact on me, as I didn't treat them as writings I had to memorize anymore. I saw them as texts I had to understand and once I understood them, they stuck with me and I didn't immediately forget them. There wasn't any assignments that I felt were unnecessary, one about translating whike using the methods was annoying yes, but I think they were all required and important.

İleriki seferlerde duzeltilecegini dusunuyorum ama bu ilk seferde üzerimize deney yapılmış gibi oldu ve çok yıprandık. Son senede bu kadar ağır bir ders yükü olacağını hayal edemezdim.
